commandments_title: The 10 Commandments of PII (passive income investing)

commandments.title: Thou shalt understand your assets
commandments.text: A fund is a wrapper / middleman; you own the stocks, bonds, commodities or Bitcoin inside it. Know what they are and where they are listed.

commandments.title: Thou shalt understand the income strategy
commandments.text: How much of the portfolio is written with covered calls, how far out of the money, any puts, any leverage? Providers differ (Hamilton, Harvest, BMO, Evolve, Brompton).

commandments.title: Thou shalt understand distributions and yield
commandments.text: Distributions come out of the fund's NAV (price drops by the payment on the ex-date). Yield is just an annual percentage and can change; it is not a GIC.

commandments.title: Thou shalt not ignore total returns
commandments.text: Judge performance by total return (price plus reinvested distributions), never by the price chart alone; use sensible benchmarks and identical start/end dates.

commandments.title: Thou shalt invest responsibly
commandments.text: Protect registered accounts (TFSA/RRSP/Roth/401k), keep risky bets (single stocks, Bitcoin) in a cash account, avoid crazy leverage, diversify, and set position limits.

commandments.title: Thou shalt never sell
commandments.text: Buy and hold: the distributions mean you never have to sell. Exceptions: streamlining, rebalancing, tax or strategy changes.

commandments.title: Thou shalt remain focused on the long term
commandments.text: Ignore day-to-day noise and headlines; do not panic-sell. Never selling (6) makes this easier.

commandments.title: Thou shalt reinvest accordingly
commandments.text: Reinvest as much as suits your situation (even retirees: consider 5-15%); it grows income over time.

commandments.title: Thou shalt not judge other investing strategies
commandments.text: Dividend, index, growth and covered-call investing all work for the people who stick with them.

commandments.title: Thou shalt cherish life and be generous
commandments.text: Enjoy the cash flow and be generous; money is a tool.

checklist_title: Covered call ETF checklist (his order of importance)

checklist_source.title: Covered Call ETF Checklist: how I evaluate covered call ETFs

checklist.title: Holdings
checklist.text: What is actually inside? Peel the onion for funds-of-funds (e.g. USCL holds 125% of USCC; HYLD holds SMAX; BMAX and HHIS hold baskets). "By far the most important thing."

checklist.title: Covered-call strategy
checklist.text: Maximum share of the portfolio written (Canada: nobody goes over 50%) and moneyness of the calls: how much upside am I giving up? More calls = more yield but less upside.

checklist.title: Total return
checklist.text: Compare against a matching benchmark with the same start date (USCL vs VFV, QQCL vs QQC, HYLD vs CAD-hedged S&P 500 VSP, HHIS vs Nasdaq-100). Expectation: with at most 50% coverage and modest leverage, total return should be similar to the underlying.

checklist.title: Yield
checklist.text: Useful to know how much income to expect, but "not super important" next to total return; it changes with the price and distributions can change.

checklist.title: Management fee
checklist.text: Look at the management fee, not the MER (the MER of leveraged funds includes borrowing costs). Canadian covered-call ETFs typically 0.40-0.85%, mid-range about 0.65%.

checklist.title: Currency hedging / listing
checklist.text: Is the fund hedged to the Canadian dollar (HYLD is; QQCL, HHIS and QDAY are not)? He typically prefers unhedged because he believes more in the USD; HYLD.U is the USD-unhedged listing. Pick the benchmark accordingly (HYLD vs CAD-hedged VSP).

principles.title: Yield is not return
principles.text: A 40% yield with a price down 30% is a 10% total return.

principles.title: Track your own total return
principles.text: Include income in your portfolio total return (e.g. Snowball Analytics) or red price charts will mislead you even when you are green after 3 years of DRIP.

source.title: 2 Income Investing MISTAKES to AVOID! Total Return Tracking

principles.title: Hold through crashes
principles.text: Not having to sell is the defence; buying in a flash crash is worth more than buying on the way up.

source.title: Portfolio Down 165k in ONE DAY?! Am I worried?

principles.title: Modest leverage
principles.text: He favours lightly leveraged (about 25%) covered-call ETFs, not 2x/3x daily-reset products.

source.title: Do Leveraged ETFs Make Sense for Long Term Income Investors?

principles.title: Position limits
principles.text: His examples: no more than 20% in HHIS, about 5% in Bitcoin, about 5% in gold.

principles.title: Hold-forever funds
principles.text: On HHIS: "I'm going to hold HHIS forever" (it is close to holding its underlying ~20 stocks with covered calls and 25% leverage).

source.title: HHIS: Can you Hold it FOREVER?

total_return.text: Total return = price change plus all distributions, ideally reinvested (DRIP). He says to use the same start and end date for every fund in a comparison, compare to an apples-to-apples benchmark, and never use price return alone ("that's for amateurs").

never_invest.title: 9 things he says he would never invest in (his opinion, 2026-10-14)
items: Defensive-sector ETFs (healthcare, staples, utilities) - "the best defence is not having to sell"
Physical real estate as an investment
Pure international (developed ex-US, e.g. MSCI EAFE) stocks
Spot / physical commodities (prefers commodity producers, e.g. CMCL)
Private credit: BDCs, private mortgages, fixed-income closed-end funds
Cash and cash ETFs ("cash is trash")
